title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.

report.summary: A meta-analysis of 516 multi-agent LLM configurations finds that once sample count and compute budget are matched, multi-agent coordination usually does not beat simpler single-model baselines.
report.background: Multi-agent LLM frameworks such as AutoGen, CrewAI, MetaGPT and various 'debate' or 'role-play' pipelines have become a dominant design pattern, promising better reasoning through collaboration. Yet most published evaluations compare a multi-agent system against a single greedy decoding pass, which conflates three very different things: coordination between agents, the extra samples those agents generate, and the raw inference compute spent. Meanwhile, test-time compute scaling and self-consistency ensembling have shown that simply sampling more and aggregating can deliver large gains on their own. This paper asks a simple but overdue question: if you give a single model the same number of samples or the same token/dollar budget as a multi-agent team, does the team still win? It aggregates nine empirical studies into a unified resource-vector framework with a four-rung baseline ladder to disentangle these effects.
key_points: The authors pooled nine studies covering 516 distinct multi-agent configurations and organized them along a six-dimensional 'resource vector' (samples, tokens, model calls, etc.), then compared each against four tiers of baselines, from a single greedy pass up to a fully compute-matched single model.

Against a single greedy pass, multi-agent accuracy differences are already negative on average, and essentially zero if the largest contributing study is removed. So even the headline wins are fragile and driven by one outlier.

When baselines are matched on sample count or resource budget, multi-agent systems average -0.042 accuracy, and multi-level random-effects modeling stays negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the matched baseline in 74% of comparable contrasts.

Switching the baseline from greedy decoding to a sampled one moves accuracy differences by about -0.038, meaning a large chunk of reported multi-agent gains is really just the benefit of sampling more than once.

The mechanism is informational: agents that share the same evidence cannot create new information by talking. Positive returns require partitioned evidence (each agent sees different data), external verification tools, or genuine error diversity across different models.
report.impact: This is a correction to the field's default evaluation practice rather than a refutation of multi-agent systems. For researchers and benchmark authors, it means reporting a sampled or compute-matched baseline is now necessary; the paper supplies a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities for exactly that. For developers, it argues against reaching for orchestration frameworks by default: a self-consistency ensemble or extra sampling at the same cost is often equal or better, and cheaper to debug. Multi-agent design only pays off when you deliberately engineer what the paper calls the missing ingredient, namely asymmetric information, tool-based verification, or heterogeneous models. For end users, this implies many 'AI agent team' products may be charging for coordination overhead that adds little accuracy over a single well-prompted model with more retries.
report.tools: Use the paper's own accounting utilities and reviewer checklist to audit reported gains. For hands-on replication: Inspect (UK AI Safety Institute) and lm-evaluation-harness for controlled baselines; vLLM for cheap high-throughput sampling and self-consistency; DSPy for systematically comparing single-call vs multi-stage pipelines; AutoGen, CrewAI and LangGraph as the orchestration stacks to test against matched-compute baselines. Log token spend per configuration so the resource vector stays comparable.
